title: What plants need: light and water

summary.text: Methi seeds sprout even under an upturned bowl, in the dark. But they come up yellow, not green. Plants need water to grow, and light to make their green colour and their food. Your child grows methi on three plates: dry, wet in the light, and wet in the dark. Then they watch the yellow sprouts turn green in the light.
summary.art: Three steel plates on a sunny windowsill: one with dry methi seeds, one with small green sprouts, and one half-hidden under an upturned steel bowl.

intro.hook: Peel a cabbage, one leaf at a time. The outside leaves are green. The leaves deep inside are pale, almost white. Why?
intro.text: It is the same cabbage, and the same plant. But the inside leaves grew wrapped up in the dark. The outside leaves grew in the sunlight. So does a plant need light to be green? And what else does a plant need? In this unit we grow methi seeds in the light and in the dark, and with and without water, and we watch what happens.
intro.art: A child's hands holding a cabbage cut in half, with green outer leaves and pale yellow-white leaves in the middle.

outcomes: By the end I can say two things a plant needs to grow: water and light.
By the end I can say what happens to methi sprouts in the dark: they come up yellow and thin.
By the end I can say that a plant makes their own green colour, and their own food, using light.
By the end I can tell when a plant needs water: the leaves droop and the soil is dry.
By the end I can make a guess, look carefully over a few days, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A need is something a living being must have to live and grow.
terms.example: You need water and food. A plant needs water and light.
terms.art: A child drinking from a steel tumbler next to a potted plant being watered.

terms.meaning: A sprout is a very young plant that has just come out of a seed.
terms.example: Soak methi or moong seeds, and in a day or two, tiny sprouts come out.
terms.art: A spoonful of methi seeds with tiny white roots and two small green leaves coming out.

terms.meaning: A plant wilts when they are short of water. The leaves and stem go soft and droop.
terms.example: A tulsi plant left without water on a hot day wilts. After a drink, the leaves stand up again.
terms.art: Two tulsi plants side by side: one droopy in dry soil, one standing up straight in damp soil.

terms.meaning: Sunlight is the light that comes from the Sun. Plants use light to make their food.
terms.example: A sunny windowsill gets lots of sunlight. A closed cupboard gets none.
terms.art: A beam of sunlight coming through a window onto a pot of green methi.

explanations.definition: Every plant needs water to live and grow. A dry seed only starts to sprout once they soak up water.
explanations.description: A plant drinks water through their roots. The water keeps the stems and leaves firm. Without water they wilt: the leaves droop and go soft. A dry seed waits for months, and starts to sprout once they soak up water. Too much water is not good either, because roots that sit in water for days can rot.
examples: Methi seeds on a dry plate stay just as they are. On a wet plate, they sprout in a day or two.
A tulsi plant wilts on a hot day without water, and stands up again after a drink.
Rice fields in Thanjavur and Kerala are kept full of water while the young rice plants grow.
explanations.context: This card says why a plant needs water.
explanations.art: A plant's roots drinking water from damp soil, with small blue arrows going up the stem to the leaves.

explanations.definition: Green plants make their own food in their leaves, using light, air and water.
explanations.description: Humans and other animals eat food. Plants make their own food in their green leaves, and they need light to do it. A seed has a little food stored inside, so a sprout can grow for a few days in the dark. But they come up yellow and thin, and without light they grow weak.
examples: Methi under an upturned bowl sprouts, but comes up yellow and thin.
The inside leaves of a cabbage grow in the dark and are pale.
House plants grow best near a window.
explanations.context: This card says why a plant needs light.
explanations.art: A green leaf in sunlight, with a beam of light shining onto the leaf and a small picture of a food box inside the leaf.

explanations.concept: A sprout makes their green in the light
explanations.description: The green in a leaf is made by the plant. Methi makes their green only when they sense light. In the dark a sprout stays yellow and stretches tall. Put it in the light, and within a day it turns green. Scientists agree that light sets this off. They argue about how to describe what the plant does.
examples: Yellow methi sprouts from under the bowl turn green within a day on the windowsill.
Moong sprouts sold in a closed packet are white and yellow, and turn green if left in the light.
Farmers tie leaves over a cauliflower so the white part stays white.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists who study how plants sense
perspectives.explanation: The sprout senses the light and chooses to change. The sprout makes green leaves only when there is light to use them. That is a sensible choice.
Light sets off a chemical switch inside the sprout. The switch works the same way every time. They call this a response, and they do not call it a choice.

explanations.context: This card says how a yellow sprout becomes green.
explanations.art: A row of methi sprouts: yellow on the left, pale green in the middle, bright green on the right, with a sun above the green ones.

agreed.text: Plants need water to live and grow.
agreed.evidence: Seeds without water do not sprout. Plants without water wilt and, after many days, dry up. Farmers everywhere water their crops or plant them when the rains come.

agreed.text: Green plants need light to make their food.
agreed.evidence: Plants kept in the dark grow yellow and weak, and in the end they die. Plants in the light keep growing. Scientists have tested this in many experiments.

agreed.text: Plants make their green colour in the light.
agreed.evidence: Sprouts of methi, moong and many other plants grow yellow in the dark and turn green within a day when light reaches them.

challenging.claim: Plants eat soil, so a plant in soil does not need light.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Plants grow in soil, and their roots go deep into it.
challenging.against: Plants make their own food in their leaves, using light, air and water. Roots take in water and tiny bits called minerals from the soil. A plant in good soil but kept in the dark still grows yellow and weak.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that plants get their food from the soil.

challenging.claim: The more water you give a plant, the better they grow.
challenging.who: A common idea, especially when we love our plants
challenging.for: Plants need water, and a plant without water wilts.
challenging.against: Roots need air as well as water. If the soil stays soggy for days, the roots cannot get air and can rot. Most pot plants grow best when the soil is damp, not soaking.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that more water is always better.

challenging.who: A common guess before people try it
challenging.for: Plants need light to grow well, so it seems that seeds would need light too.
challenging.against: Methi, moong and many other seeds sprout in the dark, using the food stored inside the seed. A few kinds of seed, like some lettuce seeds, do need light to sprout.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that seeds need light to start.

big_questions.q: The yellow methi sprouts turned green in the light. Who made the green?
big_questions.hint: Nobody painted the sprouts. Think about what changed, and what stayed the same.

big_questions.q: How does a sprout under a bowl know there is no light?
big_questions.hint: Plants have light sensors all over their bodies. You have light sensors too. Where are yours?

big_questions.q: We need food, and plants make food. What would we eat if there were no sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Think about rice, dal, bananas and milk. Where did each one come from?

big_questions.q: Why do the leaves of a plant on a shelf lean towards the window?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the light comes from. What does the plant need from the light?

story.title: The Red Bucket on the Balcony
story.note: Lakshmi, Kannan and Paati are made up. Methi sprouts grown in the dark really are yellow, and really turn green within about a day in the light.
text: Lakshmi lived in a flat in Mysuru, on the third floor. She was six. Her little brother Kannan was four. Their grandmother, Paati, lived with them.

On the balcony there was an old steel tray full of soil. One Sunday, Paati gave Lakshmi a handful of methi seeds. The seeds were small, hard and yellow-brown. 'Scatter them all over the soil,' said Paati. 'Then sprinkle a little water on top.'
Lakshmi scattered the seeds. She sprinkled the water with her fingers, like rain. 'How long will they take?' she asked.
'Keep the soil damp, and you will see,' said Paati.
Kannan was watching. He had a red plastic bucket from the beach. He turned the bucket upside down on one corner of the tray. 'This is my bucket's house,' he said. 'Nobody can move it.'
Paati laughed and let it be.

Every morning, Lakshmi sprinkled water on the tray. On Tuesday, she saw tiny white roots poking out of the seeds. On Wednesday, little stems stood up. On Thursday, each sprout opened two small round leaves. They were bright green, like new bangles.
On Friday morning, Kannan wanted his bucket back. He lifted it up, and he shouted. 'Akka! Come and see! Ghost plants!'
Lakshmi ran out. Under the bucket, there were sprouts too. But they were not green at all. They were pale yellow, and very tall and thin. Some of them had fallen over.
'Are they sick?' asked Kannan. 'Are they a different plant?'
Lakshmi looked closely. The seeds under the bucket were the same methi seeds. The soil under the bucket was the same soil, and it was still damp. She thought hard. What was different?
'It was dark under the bucket,' she said slowly. 'The bucket kept the sunlight out.'
Paati nodded. 'So what should we do now?'
'Leave the bucket off,' said Lakshmi. 'Let the light in, and see what happens.'
That night, Kannan did not want to sleep. 'Will the ghost plants still be there?' he asked. 'Will they be sad?'

Next morning, Lakshmi and Kannan ran to the balcony before breakfast. The pale corner was not pale any more. The tall, thin sprouts had turned light green, like the inside of a cucumber. By the evening, they were as green as the rest.
'Who painted them?' asked Kannan.

'Nobody,' said Lakshmi. 'The methi made the green themselves. They only make it when they feel the light.' Kannan put his hand flat over one sprout, like a tiny roof. 'Now it is dark for you,' he whispered. Then he took his hand away. 'And now it is light again.'
Paati smiled. 'Plants feel the light, just as your skin feels the sun. In a week, we will pick the methi leaves and put them in the dal.'
Kannan put his bucket away in the cupboard. 'My bucket's house can be in there,' he said. 'The methi needs the sun more than my bucket does.'
story.epiphany: Lakshmi works out that the only difference under the bucket was the dark. When the light comes back, the methi makes their own green.
ask: Why were the sprouts under the bucket yellow?
The soil under the bucket was still damp. Why does that matter?
What do you think Kannan's sprout felt under his hand?
art: A girl sprinkling water with her fingers over a steel tray of soil on a balcony, with her little brother holding a red bucket.
A boy lifting a red bucket off one corner of a tray of green sprouts, showing tall pale yellow sprouts underneath.
The same tray the next evening: all the sprouts green, and the boy holding his hand like a little roof over one sprout.

games.title: What Does Methi Need?
games.players: 1 to 4 players and a grown-up who reads the backs
games.context: This is a sorting game about what a plant needs. Each card names something. Players decide if the methi needs it to grow (green basket) or not (grey basket).

items.b: Green basket. Methi needs this. Plants make their food using light.
Green basket. Methi needs this. Seeds need water to sprout, and plants need water to grow.
Green basket. Methi needs this. Rain is water for plants.
Green basket. Light from a bright lamp also works, though sunlight is stronger.
Green basket. Methi needs this. Plants use air to make food, and their roots need air too.
Grey basket. Not needed. Plants make their own sugar in their leaves. We do not have to feed them sugar.
Grey basket. Not needed. Milk is food for young mammals, not for plants.
Grey basket. Not needed. A plant has no use for a toy car.

items.f: An upturned steel bowl over the plant
items.b: Grey basket. Not good. The bowl blocks the light, and the sprouts come up yellow.
Grey basket. Not good. In the dark, a plant cannot make food.
Grey basket. Too much. Roots in soggy soil for days can rot. Damp is just right.
Grey basket. Not good. A plant in dry soil wilts.
Grey basket. Not needed. Plants make their own food.
Green basket. This gives the plant the water they need.

printables.title: 2 basket labels to cut out
items: GREEN BASKET: Methi needs this. (Draw a sun and a water drop.)
GREY BASKET: Not needed, or not good. (Draw a cross.)

rules: Put the two labels on the floor, a little apart. Mix the 14 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. The grown-up turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. Think: does the methi need this?
Put the card on the green label or the grey label, and say why.
The grown-up reads the back. If you were right, you score 1 point and the card stays there. If you were wrong, the grown-up moves the card to the right label and nobody scores.
The game ends when the pile is finished. Count your points. The most points wins; if it is a tie, everyone wins. With one player, see how many you got right.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper on the floor with two labels, a green one and a grey one, and a pile of face-down cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two labels. Mix the cards.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that says 'A packet of sugar', about to put it on the grey label.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, say why, and put it on a label.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 14 cards and the 2 labels. 2. Put the labels on the floor. 3. Mix the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: This game is about what a plant needs. The green label is for things the methi needs. The grey label is for things they don't need.
flow.kid: Look at the two labels. Green is for what methi needs. Grey is for what methi does not need.

flow.do: Take turns. The grown-up reads a card aloud. The child puts it on a label and says why. The grown-up reads the back and gives a point if the child was right.
flow.say: What does the card say? Does the methi need it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Does methi need this? Put it on a label. Say why.

ask.q: Why does the packet of sugar go on the grey label?
good: Plants make their own sugar.
Plants make their own food, so they don't need us to feed them.

flow.do: At the end, look at the cards on the green label together. Ask your child what they have in common.
flow.say: Look at all the cards on the green label. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Look at the green label. What does methi need?

check.q: Which one does a plant need?
check.why: A plant needs light to make their own food. Biscuits and milk are food for humans and other animals, not for plants.

games.title: Green or Yellow?
games.context: This is a guessing game about light. Each card says where a methi sprout grew. Players guess if the sprout will be green or yellow, by holding up a green or a yellow crayon.

items.b: Green. There is lots of light.
Yellow. Steel blocks all the light.

items.f: Under an upturned clear glass bowl
items.b: Green. Light goes through clear glass.
Yellow. No light gets in.
Yellow. It is dark inside.

items.f: On a table under a bright lamp, all day
items.b: Green. A bright lamp gives light.
Green. Light goes through clear plastic.

items.f: Inside a cardboard shoebox with the lid shut
items.b: Yellow. Cardboard blocks the light.

items.f: On the balcony, in the morning sun
items.b: Green. There is lots of light.

items.f: Under a thick doormat for a week
items.b: Yellow. The mat blocks the light.

items.f: Under a bowl for 4 days, then on the windowsill for 1 day
items.b: Green. The yellow sprouts turn green within a day in the light.
Yellow. A thick black cloth blocks the light.

rules: Each player has a green crayon and a yellow crayon. One person is the reader (with two people, the grown-up reads).
The reader mixes the cards and reads one out loud, starting 'A methi sprout grew…'. Keep the back hidden from the players.
Everyone holds up green or yellow at the same time.
The reader reads the back. Everyone who was right scores 1 point.
The game ends when all 12 cards are read. The most points wins; if it is a tie, everyone wins. To play again, someone else is the reader.

setup.art: Two children each holding up a green crayon and a yellow crayon, and a grown-up holding a card.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone has a green and a yellow crayon.

setup.art: A card saying 'Under an upturned steel bowl' and a child holding up a yellow crayon.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to the place. Hold up green or yellow.

flow.do: Give each player a green and a yellow crayon. Mix the cards.
flow.say: I will tell you where a methi sprout grew. You guess: will the sprout be green or yellow?
flow.kid: Hold a green crayon and a yellow crayon. Listen to where the sprout grew.

flow.do: Read each card. Everyone shows a crayon. Read the back and give points.
flow.say: A methi sprout grew under a clear glass bowl. Green or yellow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen. Green or yellow? Hold one up. Then say why.

ask.q: Why is the sprout under the clear glass bowl green?
good: Light goes through clear glass.
The sprout still gets light.

flow.do: Ask your child to make up one new place card of their own.
flow.say: Make up a new place for a sprout. Can you trick me?
flow.kid: Make up a new place for a sprout. Ask a grown-up: green or yellow?

check.q: Which of these keeps a methi sprout yellow?
options: A clear glass bowl over it
A shoebox with the lid shut
check.why: A shut shoebox lets no light in. Under a clear glass bowl or on a sunny windowsill, the sprout gets light and turns green.

experiments.title: Three Plates of Methi: dry, light and dark
experiments.context: In this experiment you put methi seeds on three plates. One plate stays dry. One is wet and in the light. One is wet and under a bowl, in the dark. Over six days, you watch what happens on each plate.
experiments.question: Do methi seeds need water to sprout? What happens to methi sprouts that get water but no light?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which plate will sprout? Which sprouts will be green, and which will not? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three plates get the same seeds, from one packet, on the same tissue, in the same place. Plate 1 and plate 2 are different only in water. Plate 2 and plate 3 are different only in light.
results_table: Day 6: after a day in the light

materials.item: 3 small steel plates or katoris, all the same
kitchen tissue or an old cotton hanky, folded to fit each plate
an upturned steel bowl or dabba that covers plate 3 completely
a spoon and a cup of water
3 small paper labels with drawings: a crossed-out drop, a sun and a drop, a bowl and a drop

schedule.what: Set up the three plates. Guess what will happen.
Look at plates 1 and 2. Add 2 spoons of water to plates 2 and 3. Lift the bowl only for a moment.
Look at plate 2. Add 2 spoons of water to plates 2 and 3.
Add 2 spoons of water to plates 2 and 3. Look at plate 2.
Lift the bowl. Compare all three plates. Leave plate 3 uncovered on the windowsill.
Look at plate 3 again. Have the yellow sprouts changed colour?

experiments.record: Draw the three plates on day 5. Colour the sprouts the colour you see. Draw plate 3 again on day 6.

setup.art: Three steel plates in a row, each with a folded tissue and a small spoonful of methi seeds, the first tissue dry and the other two wet.
setup.caption: 1. Put one teaspoon of seeds on each plate. Wet plates 2 and 3 only.

setup.art: The three plates on a bright windowsill, with an upturned steel bowl covering plate 3.
setup.caption: 2. Put all three by a bright window. Cover plate 3 with a bowl.

setup.art: A hand lifting the steel bowl to show tall yellow sprouts, next to a plate of short green sprouts and a plate of dry seeds.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, lift the bowl and compare.

flow.do: 1. Fold a tissue onto each plate. 2. Pour 3 spoons of water on plates 2 and 3. Leave plate 1 dry. 3. Sprinkle one teaspoon of methi seeds on each plate, spread out. 4. Draw a small label for each plate (a crossed-out drop, a sun and a drop, a bowl and a drop) and put it beside the plate.
flow.say: Here are three plates of methi seeds. Plate 1 stays dry. Plates 2 and 3 get water. Help me spread the seeds out.
flow.kid: Put a tissue on each plate. Wet plates 2 and 3. Keep plate 1 dry. Sprinkle seeds on each plate.
flow.parent: Use seeds from one packet for all three plates. The tissue on plates 2 and 3 should be wet but with no puddle.

flow.do: 1. Put all three plates on a bright windowsill. 2. Turn the steel bowl upside down over plate 3, so no light gets in.
flow.say: Plate 3 goes under the bowl. Now it is dark in there. Plates 1 and 2 stay in the light.
flow.kid: Put the plates by the window. Cover plate 3 with the bowl. Now plate 3 is in the dark.
flow.parent: Choose a bright place out of hot afternoon sun. A steel bowl in strong sun gets hot and can cook the seeds. Set the bowl flat on the sill, so no light slips in under the edge.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess for each plate, and to say why. You write the guesses down.
flow.say: Which plate will sprout? What colour will the sprouts be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which plate will sprout? Green or not? Why?

good: The dry seeds won't grow, because seeds need water.
The ones under the bowl won't grow, because there's no light.
The ones in the light will be green.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Many children guess that the seeds under the bowl will not sprout at all. Don't say what will happen.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow, on day 2. Do the same on days 3 and 4 (3 minutes each day).
flow.do: 1. Look at plates 1 and 2. 2. Add 2 spoons of water to plates 2 and 3. Lift the bowl only for a moment to add the water.
flow.say: Look closely at plate 1 and plate 2. What has changed?
flow.kid: Look at plate 1. Look at plate 2. What is different? Add water to plates 2 and 3.

ask.q: What do you see on plate 2?
good: Tiny white roots coming out.
The seeds got bigger.

flow.parent: Wet methi seeds usually show tiny white roots within one or two days. The dry seeds stay the same. Days 3 and 4 are the same: look, then water plates 2 and 3. The tissue must stay wet, never dry.

flow.do: 1. Lift the bowl off plate 3. 2. Put the three plates side by side. 3. Look at the colour and the height of the sprouts on each plate. 4. Draw them. 5. Leave plate 3 uncovered on the windowsill.
flow.say: Let's lift the bowl. What do you see? How are plate 2 and plate 3 different?
flow.kid: Lift the bowl. Look at plate 3. Look at plate 2. What is different?

ask.q: Plates 2 and 3 both got water. So why are they different?
good: Plate 3 was in the dark.
There was no light under the bowl.

check.q: The sprouts under the bowl had water, but no light. What colour were they?
check.why: In the dark, methi sprouts come up yellow and thin. They made no green, because there was no light.

flow.parent: Sprouts from the dark are yellow, taller and thinner, and may lean over. If plate 3 has no sprouts, the seeds were too dry or too hot: try again with more water, out of the sun.

flow.do: 1. Look at plate 3 again, after a day in the light. 2. Put it next to your drawing from yesterday.
flow.say: Yesterday these sprouts were yellow. Look at them now. What happened? Who made the change?
flow.kid: Look at plate 3 again. Are the sprouts still yellow? What changed?

ask.q: Why did the sprouts turn green?
good: Because they got light.
The methi made the green when the light came.

flow.parent: Most yellow sprouts turn light green within a day in the light, and greener the day after. If they still look yellow, wait one more day. Methi needs water to sprout, and light to turn green.

activities.title: Plant Spotting at Home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find every plant. For each plant, you look at where they live and how much light they get.

schedule.what: Find every plant at home or outside the window. Look at where each one lives.

activities.record: Draw one plant and the window nearest to them.

setup.art: A child walking through a flat, pointing at a money plant by a window and a tulsi pot on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home. Find every plant.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a potted plant next to a window with a big yellow sun.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one plant and their window.

flow.do: Walk round the home together. Look for every plant: pots, a money plant, tulsi, herbs, or trees outside the window.
flow.say: Let's find every plant in our home. Where does each one live?
flow.kid: Find every plant in your home. Look out of the windows too.
flow.parent: If you have no plants at home, look out of the window at trees, or at plants on other balconies.

flow.do: For each plant, ask: is this plant near a window? Is the soil dry or damp? Then draw one plant.
flow.say: Is this plant near a window? Why do you think we put plants there?
flow.kid: Is this plant near a window? Why? Draw one plant.

ask.q: Why do we keep plants near windows?
good: Because plants need light.
The light comes in through the window.

activities.title: The Cabbage Puzzle: green outside, pale inside
activities.context: In this activity you peel a cabbage leaf by leaf, and line up the leaves from the outside to the inside. You look at how the colour changes, and work out why.

materials.item: a cabbage, or half a cabbage
a big plate or a clean floor mat

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the cabbage in half with a knife.

schedule.what: Peel the cabbage leaves and line them up. Find out why the inside is pale.

activities.record: Colour a row of leaves from dark green to pale.

setup.art: A child peeling the outer green leaf off a cabbage over a big steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Peel the leaves one by one.

setup.art: A row of cabbage leaves on a mat, from big dark green on the left to small pale yellow on the right.
setup.caption: 2. Line them up, outside to inside.

flow.do: 1. Peel 6 or 7 leaves off the cabbage, one by one. 2. Lay them in a row, from the first leaf to the last.
flow.say: Let's peel the cabbage, one leaf at a time. Put each new leaf next to the last one.
flow.kid: Peel one leaf. Put it down. Peel the next one. Make a row.

flow.do: Ask your child to look along the row. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look along the row. What do you notice about the colours? Why do you think that happens?
flow.kid: Look at the row. Which leaves are green? Which are pale? Why?

ask.q: Why are the inside leaves pale?
good: They were in the dark.
The outside leaves covered them, so no light got in.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own idea before you say anything.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the cabbage in half. 2. Look at the inside together.
flow.say: Look inside. The leaves are wrapped tightly, like a ball. Could the light get in here?
flow.kid: Look inside the cabbage. The leaves are wrapped tight. Can light get in?

check.q: Which cabbage leaves got the most light while the cabbage grew?
check.why: The outside leaves covered the others, so they got the light. The leaves in the middle sat in the dark, wrapped up, and stayed pale.

flow.parent: Cook the cabbage afterwards. Nothing goes to waste.

activities.title: Light Through or Light Blocked?
activities.context: In this activity you shine a torch through things from the kitchen. You find out which ones let light through and which ones block the light. Then you guess which ones would keep methi sprouts yellow.

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
a steel plate, a clear glass, a clear plastic bag, a piece of cardboard and a thin cotton cloth

schedule.what: Shine the torch through each thing. Sort them into 'light goes through' and 'light is blocked'.

activities.record: Draw the things that block the light in one box, and the things that let light through in another box.

setup.art: A child shining a torch at a clear glass held in front of a wall, with a bright spot on the wall behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch through each thing at a wall.

setup.art: Two piles on a table: a steel plate and cardboard in one, a clear glass and a plastic bag in the other.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them into two piles.

flow.do: 1. Dim the room. 2. Hold each thing in front of a wall. 3. Shine the torch at it from the other side. 4. Look for light on the wall.
flow.say: Hold the clear glass in front of the wall. I'll shine the torch. Do you see light on the wall?
flow.kid: Hold one thing up. Shine the torch on it. Is there light on the wall?
flow.parent: The thin cloth lets some light through. Put it in its own pile: some light. Methi under it would be partly green.

ask.q: Would methi under a clear glass be yellow or green?
good: Green, because the light gets through.

projects.title: Grow Methi to Eat
projects.context: In this project you grow a small tray of methi on the windowsill. You give the methi water and light. After about twelve days, you snip the leaves and eat them.

materials.item: a small tray, an old plastic box with holes poked in the bottom, or a pot
soil from a pot plant, or a few layers of wet tissue if you have no soil

schedule.what: Soak the seeds for a few hours. Fill the tray, scatter the seeds, and sprinkle with water.
Look for sprouts. Sprinkle water so the soil stays damp.
Count the leaves on one sprout. Draw your tray.
Sprinkle water. Are the plants leaning towards the window?
Snip the methi with scissors. Wash the leaves and add them to dal, or to an uttapam or a thepla.

projects.record: Draw your methi tray on day 1, day 6 and day 12.

setup.art: A small plastic tray of soil on a windowsill, with a child scattering methi seeds over it.
setup.caption: 1. Scatter the seeds on damp soil.

setup.art: The same tray full of small green methi plants, and a grown-up snipping them with scissors into a steel bowl.
setup.caption: 2. After about 12 days, snip and eat.

flow.do: 1. Soak the seeds in water for 3 or 4 hours. 2. Fill the tray with damp soil. 3. Scatter the seeds thickly. 4. Press them in gently. 5. Put the tray on a bright windowsill.
flow.say: We are giving the methi everything they need. What do they need?
flow.kid: Scatter the seeds on the soil. Press them in. Put the tray by the window.

ask.q: What will the methi need from us?
good: Water.
Light, so the tray goes by the window.

flow.wait: Come back every morning. Look closely on days 3, 6 and 9.
flow.do: Each morning, touch the soil and sprinkle a little water if it feels dry. On days 3, 6 and 9, look closely. On day 6, count the leaves on one sprout and draw the tray.
flow.say: Feel the soil. Is it damp or dry? How much water should we give?
flow.kid: Touch the soil. Is it dry? Then sprinkle a little water.
flow.parent: Water with a spoon, or with the gentle-rain bottle if you made one. A strong pour knocks the small sprouts over.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up snips the methi just above the soil. 2. Wash the leaves. 3. Cook them in dal, or in an uttapam or a thepla.
flow.say: These leaves were made from water, air and sunlight. Now they will be part of our lunch.
flow.kid: A grown-up snips the methi. Wash the leaves. Help cook them.

challenges.title: A Gentle Rain for Tiny Sprouts
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Small sprouts fall over when you pour water on them. Can you make a watering bottle that rains gently?
challenges.problem: Methi sprouts are tiny and thin. If you pour water from a cup, they fall over. Make a waterer that sprinkles water as gently as light rain.
constraints: Water at least 10 sprouts without knocking any over.
materials: an empty plastic bottle with a cap
a safety pin or a thumbtack, for a grown-up to make holes
a tray or plate of methi sprouts (from the methi test or the methi tray)
general: Poke 5 or 6 small holes in the bottle cap. Turn the bottle upside down and squeeze gently.
Dip your fingers in water and flick the drops onto the sprouts.
Use a spoon and let the water drip off the edge.
creative: Poke tiny holes in the bottom of a plastic cup. Hold the cup over the sprouts and pour water into the cup.
Soak a sponge or a clean cloth and squeeze it gently over the sprouts.
Stand the pot in a plate of water, so the soil drinks from the bottom up.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own gentle rain. Draw it, make it, and test it. Did any sprouts fall over?

setup.art: A grown-up's hands poking small holes in a plastic bottle cap with a safety pin.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pokes small holes in the cap.

setup.art: A child squeezing an upside-down bottle so a fine spray of drops falls on small methi sprouts.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze gently over the sprouts.

flow.do: Pour water from a cup onto wet tissue with some methi sprouts. Use sprouts from the methi test or the methi tray. Watch what happens.
flow.say: Watch what a big pour does to the tiny sprouts. How could we make the water fall more gently?
flow.kid: Pour water from a cup. What happens to the sprouts? How can you be gentler?

flow.kid: Count the sprouts still standing. What would you change?

ask.q: Why is a gentle rain better for tiny sprouts?
good: Big pours knock them over.
The sprouts are thin and weak.

items.why: Plants need water, light and air. They make their own food, so they do not need sweets or milk.
items.art: Six small pictures: a water drop, a sun, a laddu, a toy car, swirls of air and a glass of milk.

items.p: Remember the three plates of methi? On day 2, what came out of the wet seeds on plate 2?
items.why: Wet seeds soak up water, swell and put out a tiny white root first. The leaves come later.

items.p: Draw the methi sprouts from under the bowl, and the methi sprouts from the window. Colour them the colours you saw.
items.a: Tall, thin, yellow sprouts for the bowl. Short sprouts with green leaves for the window.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both the colour and the shape: the sprouts in the dark are yellow and taller and thinner.
items.art: Two empty plates, one with a bowl drawn above it and one with a sun.

items.p: Draw a line from each plant to what they need.
pairs: A droopy tulsi in dry soil
Dry methi seeds in a jar
items.why: A plant with droopy leaves and dry soil needs water. Yellow sprouts need light. Dry seeds need water to sprout.
items.art: A droopy tulsi plant, a cupboard with yellow sprouts inside, a jar of seeds, a water drop and a sun.

items.p: Methi can grow green leaves in a dark cupboard.
items.why: False. Methi makes their green only in the light. In a dark cupboard the sprouts come up yellow.

items.p: First draw your three plates from day 5 (or look at your drawing). Then write 1, 2 or 3 under each. 1 is dry. 2 is wet in the light. 3 is wet under the bowl.
items.a: 1 under the dry seeds, 2 under the short green sprouts, 3 under the tall yellow sprouts.
items.why: Dry seeds did not sprout. Wet seeds in the light grew green. Wet seeds in the dark grew yellow.
items.art: Three plates in a mixed-up order: tall yellow sprouts, dry seeds, short green sprouts.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: plates 2 and 3 both got water. Why were their sprouts different colours?
items.a: Plate 3 was under the bowl, in the dark. Plate 2 was in the light. Methi makes green only in the light.
items.why: A strong answer says that light was the only difference between plate 2 and plate 3.

items.p: Which one does NOT help a plant grow?
items.why: A dark cupboard keeps light away. The sunny window, the watering can and the rain all give the plant something they need.

items.p: Put these methi steps in order, from first to last.
items: A tiny white root comes out
a: A tiny white root comes out
items.why: First the seed soaks up water. Then the root comes out. Then the stem and the first leaves.
items.art: Three pictures: a methi sprout with two small leaves, a dry seed, a seed with a tiny white root.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi lift the bowl and see tall yellow methi sprouts.

views.says: These sprouts are sick. We should throw them away.
These sprouts are fine. They are only waiting for light.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you saw on day 6. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Revathi is closer: on day 6, the yellow sprouts turned green in the light. But Fathima is right that they are weaker: they are thin and some fell over.
items.why: A strong answer uses the day 6 result, and is fair to both: the sprouts were alive and could turn green, but they were thin and weak.

items.p: Anu, a girl in Class 1, puts methi seeds on wet tissue under a clear glass bowl. What colour will the sprouts be?
items.why: Light goes through clear glass, so the sprouts still get light. They will be green.

items.p: Draw a line from each sign to what the plant is short of.
pairs: Soft brown roots in soggy soil
items.why: Yellow, thin sprouts and pale leaves mean little light. Droopy leaves and dry soil mean little water. Roots in soggy soil cannot get air.

items.p: Sort these: does light go through, or is the light blocked?
items.why: Light passes through clear glass and clear plastic. Steel and cardboard block it, so a sprout under them is in the dark.

items.p: The pale leaves deep inside a cabbage are pale because little light reached them.
items.why: True. The inside leaves grow wrapped up by the outer leaves. With little light, they make little green.

items.p: Draw a plant who has water but no light. Next to it, draw a plant who has light but no water.
items.a: A tall, thin, yellow plant in damp soil, in a dark place. A droopy plant with dry soil in the sun.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two different signs: no light gives yellow and thin, no water gives droopy and dry.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a girl in your class wants to grow methi inside a closed cupboard. What would you tell her?
items.a: The methi will sprout, but they will be yellow and thin. Put them by a window, so they get light and turn green.
items.why: A strong answer says what will happen in the dark and gives a way to fix it.

items.p: Draw a methi sprout. Then label the parts: root, stem, leaf. Write each word, or ask a grown-up to write it.
items.a: The root is the white part at the bottom. The stem is in the middle. The leaves are at the top.
items.why: The root takes in water. The stem holds the leaves up. The leaves catch the light.
items.art: A large drawing of a methi sprout with a white root, a thin stem and two round leaves, with three empty label lines.

items.p: Draw 5 green sprouts and 3 yellow sprouts. Which colour did you draw more of?
items.a: There are more green sprouts: 5 is more than 3.
items.why: 5 is more than 3. A strong answer counts the drawing and says which colour has more.
items.art: A plate with 5 short green methi sprouts on one side and 3 tall yellow sprouts on the other.

items.p: Put the steps of the three plates test in order.
items: Put the seeds on the plates
Wet the tissue on plates 2 and 3
a: Wet the tissue on plates 2 and 3
Put the seeds on the plates
items.why: First wet the tissue and add the seeds, then cover plate 3. Look at the end.

items.p: Rina, a girl in Class 1, keeps her methi tray by the window. For a week, the soil stays soggy. What may happen to the roots? What should she do? Say your answer to a grown-up.
items.a: The roots may rot, because they cannot get air. She should stop watering until the soil is only damp, and let extra water drain away.
items.why: A strong answer says roots need air as well as water, and gives a way to fix it.

items.p: A tulsi plant on the balcony has droopy leaves. The soil is dry and cracked. What does the tulsi need?
items.why: Droopy leaves and dry soil mean the plant is short of water. A drink will help the leaves stand up again.

quiz.p: What do plants need to grow?
quiz.why: Plants need light and water. They make their own food, so they do not need sweets or milk.

quiz.p: Methi seeds sat on a dry plate for two days. What happened?
quiz.why: Seeds need water to sprout. Dry seeds stay as they are.

quiz.p: Methi sprouts grew under an upturned steel bowl. What did they look like?
quiz.why: In the dark, methi sprouts come up yellow, tall and thin.

quiz.p: The yellow sprouts were put on the windowsill for a day. What happened?
quiz.why: In the light, the methi made their green. Most sprouts turn green within a day.

quiz.p: Who made the green in the methi leaves?
quiz.why: The plant makes their own green, when they sense light.

quiz.p: Where do plants make their food?
quiz.why: Plants make food in their green leaves, using light, air and water. Many people think plants eat soil, but the roots only take in water and minerals.

quiz.p: A plant has droopy leaves and dry soil. What does the plant need?
quiz.why: Droopy leaves and dry soil mean the plant is short of water.

quiz.p: Is a soggy pot that never dries good for a plant?
opts: Yes, more water is always better
quiz.why: Roots in soggy soil for days cannot get air and can rot. Damp soil is just right.

quiz.p: Before you lifted the bowl, what did a good scientist do first?
opts: Guessed what would happen, and said why
quiz.why: Scientists guess first, then look carefully, then say what they saw.

quiz.p: Two plates of methi seeds get the same water. One is under a bowl, one is in the light. Why give them the same water?
opts: So that light was the only difference
quiz.why: When only one thing is different, we know that thing made the change. Here, the only difference was light.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a plant to feel light?
open_questions.why_open: Plants have light sensors, and they answer the light. But nobody knows what feeling light is like for a plant.

open_questions.q: Why are most plants green, and not black?
open_questions.why_open: A black leaf could take in more of the light. Scientists have several ideas about why leaves are green, and they still argue about it.

open_questions.q: Could we grow plants on Mars?
open_questions.why_open: Mars gets less sunlight, and the soil and air are very different. Scientists are testing plants in Mars-like soil on Earth, but nobody has grown a plant on Mars yet.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 1, counts 10 methi seeds onto a wet plate. On day 2, 8 of them have tiny white roots. How many do not have roots yet?
maths.answer: 2 seeds do not have roots yet.
maths.explain: 10 seeds take away 8 seeds with roots leaves 2. Seeds wake up at different times, so the last 2 may sprout tomorrow.
maths.context: This is about plate 2 in the three plates of methi test.
maths.why_maths: Counting the seeds that sprouted, and the ones that did not, tells us if almost all the seeds woke up.

maths.problem: On day 5, a green sprout from the window was 3 fingers tall. A yellow sprout from under the bowl was 5 fingers tall. Which sprout was taller? Why do you think so?
maths.answer: The yellow sprout from under the bowl was taller.
maths.explain: 5 fingers is more than 3 fingers. Sprouts in the dark stretch up tall and thin, as if looking for light.
maths.context: This is about plates 2 and 3 in the three plates of methi test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two heights shows that the dark sprouts were taller, but taller did not mean stronger.

maths.problem: The bowl stayed on plate 3 from day 1 to day 5. How many days is that?
maths.answer: 4 days, from the morning of day 1 to the morning of day 5.
maths.explain: Count on from day 1: day 2, day 3, day 4, day 5. That is 4 jumps, so 4 days.
maths.context: This is about plate 3, which sat under a bowl in the three plates of methi test.
maths.why_maths: Counting days tells us how long the sprouts were in the dark.

maths.problem: Meena, a girl in Class 1, sorted the game cards. She had 6 cards in the green basket and 8 cards in the grey basket. Which basket had more cards?
maths.answer: The grey basket had more, with 8 cards.
maths.explain: 8 is more than 6. A plant needs only a few things: light, water and air. Rain, a lamp and a watering can are ways to give them.
maths.context: This is about the game What Does Methi Need?, where you sort cards into a green basket and a grey basket.

founder: ideas/by_topic/plants.md: Photosynthesis and vision row ('grow a potted plant in varying light and record growth'; 'light is life's bridge'). Its sunbeam dance was not used, because Level 3 of this unit already has a seedling dance.
science: Etiolation and de-etiolation: seedlings grown in the dark are pale yellow with long stems and closed seed leaves, and turn green within hours to a day in light. Any plant physiology textbook (for example Taiz and Zeiger, Plant Physiology).

In flowering plants, the last step in making chlorophyll needs light (the enzyme protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase is light-dependent), so they cannot green in the dark. Many conifers and algae can make chlorophyll in the dark.
Inner cabbage leaves are pale because the outer leaves shade them. Cauliflower curds are 'blanched' by tying leaves over them.
Seed food reserves let seedlings grow for some days in the dark. Most seeds, including fenugreek and mung bean, germinate in the dark. Some lettuce varieties need light to germinate.
Plants have light receptors (phytochromes, cryptochromes, phototropins) in leaves, stems and roots.

Joseph Priestley's mint and candle experiment (1771). Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables, Discovering Their Great Power of Purifying the Common Air in Sunshine, and of Injuring It in the Shade and at Night (London, 1779), based on more than 500 experiments in the summer of 1779.
Rig Veda 1.115.1: 'surya atma jagatas tasthushas cha', the Sun is the self of what moves and what stays still.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, 2.3 Plants and light.

roots.context: We have seen methi grow yellow in the dark and green in the light. Now we ask what that tells us about plants, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Under the bowl, our methi sprouts came up yellow. After one day in the light, the same sprouts turned green. Nobody added any colour, so the methi made the green themselves. A plant makes their green when they sense light.
deep_truth.habit: We think of colours as fixed, like the green of a green crayon. But a leaf's green is something the plant makes, and only when light reaches them.
deep_truth.evidence: In the three plates test, methi under the bowl came up yellow while the same seeds by the window came up green. After a day uncovered on the windowsill, the yellow sprouts turned green.

three.who_am_i: Your body senses light too. Your eyes see it, and your skin slowly turns darker in strong sun.
three.what_is_life: Being alive means sensing what is around you and answering it. The methi sensed the light and made their green.
three.what_is_this_world: The same Sun lights the methi, the crow and you. Nearly all the food we eat comes from plants, which use that light.

roots.thread: The Sun lights the methi, and the methi answers by turning green. The Sun lights your eyes, and you answer by seeing colours. It lights your skin, and your skin slowly darkens. Each of us senses the light and answers it in our own way.

teachings.teaching: The Sun is the self of all that moves and all that stays still.
teachings.link: Plants stay in one place, yet they grow, turn green and make food with the Sun's light. Humans and other animals, who move, eat what plants make.

teachings.teaching: Unless drops of rain fall from the sky, not even a blade of green grass will be seen.
teachings.link: Our dry plate showed this. With no water, the methi seeds did not sprout at all.

science.text: Plants have light sensors in their leaves, stems and roots. These tell a sprout if there is light, and what colour the light is.
Plants feel light. What that feeling is like for a plant, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Many plant scientists say the methi turns green because light flips a chemical switch inside the sprout. The switch works the same way every time, so they call it a response, with no choosing.

practice.title: Light on your eyelids
practice.say: Sit facing a bright window, but not the Sun itself. Close your eyes. What colour do you see through your eyelids? Now cover your eyes with your hands. What colour now? Take your hands away. Feel the light come back. The methi felt the light come back too, when we lifted the bowl.
practice.kid: Sit by a bright window. Do not look at the Sun. Close your eyes. What colour do you see? Cover your eyes with your hands. Now take them away. Feel the light come back.

ask: When the methi turned green, who decided: the methi, or the light?
Your skin darkens in the sun, and methi turns green. How are they alike? How are they different?
If you lived under a bowl for four days, what would you miss most?
roots.art: A child sitting by a sunny window with eyes closed and face lit up, next to a plate of green methi sprouts in the same sunlight.

how_we_found_out.context: Do plants need light to do their work? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1771, Joseph Priestley, an English scientist, put a sprig of mint in a closed glass jar. A candle had burned out in that jar, and the air inside was used up. After some days, a candle could burn in the jar again. The mint had freshened the air. But when other people tried this, sometimes it worked and sometimes it did not. Nobody knew why. In the summer of 1779, Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor working in England, did more than 500 tests. He put leaves under water in glass jars. In sunlight, tiny bubbles came out of the green leaves. In the shade and at night, no bubbles came. He found that plants freshen the air only in light, and only with their green parts. In the dark, plants use up air, just as humans and other animals do. Today we know the bubbles were oxygen, which green leaves give out while they make food using light.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Priestley, an English scientist (1771); Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor working in England (1779)
how_we_found_out.when: Priestley's mint jar in 1771; Ingenhousz's tests in the summer of 1779, published the same year
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That plants freshen the air all the time, in the light and in the dark. Ingenhousz showed that green leaves do it only in light, and that in the dark plants use up air like humans and other animals.
how_we_found_out.art: Glass jars of water with green leaves inside on a sunny table, with tiny bubbles on the leaves, and one jar in shadow with no bubbles.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and a 6-year-old in a Mysuru-style city flat. Fixed: the sorting game now says the grown-up reads each card, since many children cannot read yet; worksheets no longer ask children to label or count a picture that is not printed, and ask them to draw it first; the seed-counting maths problem now matches the plates test; the long explanation cards are shorter; the thread no longer uses a stock line; the project no longer needs a bottle only made in the optional challenge; the three video entries still have no address (the validator needs three), so a person must find and watch them. Minutes, schedules and fair test checked and agree.
